metadata.title: Top 100 NumPy Interview Questions
metadata.description: Most probable NumPy interview questions compiled from the highest-traffic data-science interview banks. Weighted toward what actually gets asked in data analyst, data science and ML engineer screens — ndarray vs list, broadcasting, vectorization, views vs copies, boolean indexing, reshaping and linear algebra — with rarely-used API trivia pushed to LOW. Answers include the exact NumPy calls you are expected to name. Note: the LastMinuteNotes repo has no NumPy sheet (it covers only CN, DBMS, OOPS, OS and SQL), so this bank is built from six library-specific sources instead.

GeeksforGeeks.strength: By far the deepest bank (70+ Q); the only source that covers the querying API properly (np.where vs np.select vs np.nonzero vs np.argwhere vs np.extract), memory layout, masked arrays and structured arrays

InterviewBit.strength: Fresher → experienced progression plus a dedicated coding-questions block; strongest on the write-a-program tasks (moving average, local maxima, zero border, axis interchange) that follow the theory round

DataCamp.strength: Data-scientist framing; the practical applied questions — feature scaling, MSE, rolling statistics, memory optimization on large arrays, handling missing/infinite values, implementing K-Means

ProjectPro.full_name: ProjectPro NumPy Interview Questions for Data Analysts
ProjectPro.strength: Beginner → intermediate → advanced → coding split; good on the comparison questions (dot vs matmul, mean vs average, copy vs assignment, C-order vs F-order) and NumPy's role in feature engineering

Hirist.strength: Hiring-platform list reflecting current job-post expectations; strong on advanced indexing, memory-mapping large datasets, normalization and applying functions across axes

Devinterview.strength: ML/data-science interview repo; precise on fundamentals — ndarray attributes, contiguous memory, the exact broadcasting rules, ufunc categories and the full dtype list

frequency_legend.MOST_FREQ: Asked in almost every NumPy interview. Appears in 5-6 of the 6 sources. Master these first.
frequency_legend.MED: Asked in many interviews. Appears in 3-4 sources. Expected knowledge for 2+ years experience.
frequency_legend.LOW: Appears in 1-2 sources or is a deep-dive follow-up. Expected for senior roles or specialized interviews.

questions.question: What is NumPy and why is it used?
questions.answer: NumPy (Numerical Python) is the foundational library for numerical computing in Python. It provides the `ndarray` — a fast, memory-efficient N-dimensional array — plus vectorized mathematical operations, broadcasting, linear algebra, random number generation and Fourier transforms. Almost every data/ML library (pandas, scikit-learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch) is built on top of it or interoperates with its arrays.

questions.question: What is an ndarray?
questions.answer: The N-dimensional array object at the core of NumPy. It is homogeneous (every element shares one dtype), fixed-size at creation, and stored in a contiguous block of memory. That uniformity is exactly what lets NumPy run operations in compiled C over the whole buffer instead of looping in Python.

questions.question: How are NumPy arrays better than Python lists?
questions.answer: Arrays are homogeneous and stored contiguously, so they use far less memory than a list of boxed Python objects. They support vectorized element-wise operations (`a + b` adds arrays, whereas for lists it concatenates), broadcasting, and true multi-dimensional indexing like `arr[1, 2]`. They also carry a huge library of mathematical, statistical and linear-algebra functions. The trade-off: arrays are fixed-size and single-dtype, while lists can grow and hold anything.

questions.question: Why is NumPy faster than Python lists?
questions.answer: Four reasons. Contiguous memory means better CPU cache locality. Homogeneous dtype means no per-element type checking or pointer dereferencing. The loops run in compiled C rather than the Python interpreter, avoiding per-element bytecode overhead. And heavy operations delegate to optimized BLAS/LAPACK libraries and SIMD instructions. Typical speedups over an equivalent Python loop are 10-100×.

questions.question: What are the main attributes of an ndarray?
questions.answer: `ndim` — number of dimensions. `shape` — a tuple of the size along each axis. `size` — total number of elements (the product of shape). `dtype` — the data type of the elements. `itemsize` — bytes per element. `nbytes` — total bytes consumed (`size * itemsize`). `T` — the transposed view. `flags` — memory layout information such as C/F contiguity and whether the array owns its data.

questions.question: Difference between the shape and size attributes?
questions.answer: `shape` returns a tuple describing the dimensions — for a 3×4 array it is `(3, 4)`. `size` returns a single integer, the total element count — here `12`. Also note `len(arr)` gives only the length of the first axis (3), which is a common trip-up.

questions.question: What are the main features of NumPy?
questions.answer: The N-dimensional array object, broadcasting for operating on differently-shaped arrays, vectorized ufuncs, sophisticated indexing (basic, fancy and boolean), linear algebra via `np.linalg`, random sampling via `np.random`, Fourier transforms, and C/C++/Fortran interoperability so it can wrap existing numerical code.

questions.question: Difference between Python sequences, NumPy arrays and pandas objects?
questions.answer: Python lists/tuples are general-purpose, heterogeneous and dynamically sized, with no numeric operations. NumPy arrays are homogeneous, fixed-size, N-dimensional and built for fast numeric computation, but the axes carry no labels. Pandas Series/DataFrames wrap NumPy arrays and add labelled indexes, mixed column dtypes, and built-in handling of missing data — better for tabular analysis, at the cost of overhead.

questions.question: How do you convert a pandas DataFrame to a NumPy array and back?
questions.answer: Use `df.to_numpy()` (the modern, preferred call) or the older `df.values`; both drop the index and column labels and force a single common dtype. To go back: `pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=[...])`. For a mixed-dtype DataFrame the result becomes `object` dtype, which kills performance — select numeric columns first.

questions.question: Why is NumPy preferred over MATLAB or Octave?
questions.answer: It is free and open source, it lives inside a general-purpose language so array code sits alongside web servers, databases and ML pipelines without export steps, and it has an enormous ecosystem (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch). MATLAB has stronger built-in toolboxes and 1-based-index conventions some engineers prefer, but the licence cost and language isolation are why NumPy dominates data science.

questions.question: How does NumPy integrate with the machine learning ecosystem?
questions.answer: The ndarray is the common data interchange format. scikit-learn takes and returns NumPy arrays directly; pandas is built on them; TensorFlow and PyTorch convert to and from them nearly free of cost (`torch.from_numpy(a)` and `t.numpy()` even share memory). NumPy also does the feature engineering work before modelling — scaling, encoding, reshaping, train/test splitting — and implements the metrics.

questions.question: How do you check whether an array is empty?
questions.answer: Test the element count: `if arr.size == 0:`. Do not use `if not arr:` or `if arr:` — for any array with more than one element that raises `ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous`. Note also that `np.array([[]])` has size 0 but shape `(1, 0)`, so `size` is the reliable check.

questions.question: What are the ways to create a NumPy array?
questions.answer: From an existing sequence with `np.array([1, 2, 3])`; with filled constructors `np.zeros`, `np.ones`, `np.full`, `np.empty`, `np.eye`; from ranges with `np.arange` and `np.linspace`; randomly via `np.random.*`; from disk with `np.load`, `np.loadtxt`, `np.genfromtxt`; or shaped after an existing array with `np.zeros_like` and friends.

questions.question: How do you create 1D, 2D and 3D arrays?
questions.answer: Nest the lists one level deeper per dimension: `np.array([1,2,3])` is 1D with shape `(3,)`; `np.array([[1,2],[3,4]])` is 2D with shape `(2,2)`; `np.array([[[1,2],[3,4]],[[5,6],[7,8]]])` is 3D with shape `(2,2,2)`. Equivalently, build a flat array and reshape: `np.arange(8).reshape(2,2,2)`. Check with `arr.ndim`.

questions.question: What do np.zeros(), np.ones(), np.full() and np.empty() do?
questions.answer: `np.zeros((2,3))` fills with 0.0, `np.ones((2,3))` with 1.0, `np.full((2,3), 7)` with any constant. `np.empty((2,3))` allocates the memory without initializing it — marginally faster but the contents are arbitrary garbage, so only use it when you will overwrite every element. All accept a `dtype` argument.

questions.question: Difference between np.arange() and np.linspace()?
questions.answer: `np.arange(start, stop, step)` fixes the step size and excludes the stop value — `np.arange(0, 1, 0.25)` gives `[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]`. `np.linspace(start, stop, num)` fixes the number of points and includes the stop by default — `np.linspace(0, 1, 5)` gives `[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]`. Prefer `linspace` for floats, because floating-point accumulation in `arange` can produce an unexpected element count.

questions.question: Difference between np.array() and np.asarray()?
questions.answer: `np.array()` copies the input by default (`copy=True`). `np.asarray()` returns the input unchanged if it is already an ndarray of the right dtype, and only copies otherwise. Use `asarray` inside functions that just need to accept both lists and arrays without paying for a needless copy — but remember the caller's array may then be modified in place.

questions.question: What do np.eye() and np.identity() do?
questions.answer: `np.identity(n)` returns an n×n identity matrix. `np.eye(N, M=None, k=0)` is more general — it can be non-square and can shift the diagonal with `k` (`k=1` is the superdiagonal, `k=-1` the subdiagonal). Identity matrices show up constantly in linear algebra checks such as verifying `A @ np.linalg.inv(A)` is the identity.

questions.question: How do you create an array filled with the same value?
questions.answer: `np.full(shape, value)` is the direct way. Equivalents: `np.ones(shape) * value` (slower, and gives a float dtype), or `np.empty(shape); arr.fill(value)`. For an existing array's shape, use `np.full_like(arr, value)`.

questions.question: What are np.zeros_like(), np.ones_like() and np.full_like()?
questions.answer: They create a new array matching the shape *and* dtype of an existing one — `np.zeros_like(a)` is equivalent to `np.zeros(a.shape, dtype=a.dtype)`. Useful when building an output buffer that must line up exactly with an input, without hardcoding dimensions.

questions.question: How do you save and load NumPy arrays to and from disk?
questions.answer: `np.save('a.npy', arr)` and `np.load('a.npy')` use a fast binary format that preserves dtype and shape exactly. `np.savez('data.npz', x=a, y=b)` stores several arrays in one file (`np.savez_compressed` compresses them). For human-readable text use `np.savetxt`/`np.loadtxt`, which is far slower and loses dtype precision. Avoid `pickle`-backed loading of untrusted `.npy` files (`allow_pickle=True` can execute code).

questions.question: How do you work with an array too large to fit in memory?
questions.answer: Use `np.memmap('big.dat', dtype='float32', mode='r', shape=(n, m))` — it maps the file on disk into the address space, so slices are paged in on demand and only the touched portion consumes RAM. Complementary tactics: pick a smaller dtype (`float32` instead of `float64` halves memory), process in chunks, use in-place operations (`arr *= 2`, or `out=` on ufuncs) to avoid temporaries, and reach for Dask or HDF5 when it outgrows one machine.

questions.question: What data types does NumPy support?
questions.answer: Fixed-width numeric types: `int8/16/32/64` and unsigned `uint8/16/32/64`, `float16/32/64`, `complex64/128`, and `bool_`. Also `str_`/`unicode_` for fixed-length strings, `datetime64` and `timedelta64` for time, `object` for arbitrary Python objects (which forfeits every performance benefit), and structured dtypes for record-style data.

questions.question: Why must a NumPy array be homogeneous?
questions.answer: Because a single dtype means every element occupies the same number of bytes at a predictable offset, so NumPy can store them contiguously and let compiled C loops stride through the buffer with no type checks or pointer chasing. Mixing types would force an `object` array of Python pointers, which is exactly what a list already is — and just as slow.

questions.question: How do you convert an array from one dtype to another?
questions.answer: `arr.astype(np.float32)` returns a new array with the converted dtype (it always copies unless you pass `copy=False` and no conversion is needed). Be careful: float-to-int truncates toward zero rather than rounding, and downcasting can silently overflow — `np.array([300], dtype=np.uint8)` wraps to 44. Specify dtype at creation when you can: `np.array([1,2], dtype=np.float64)`.

questions.question: How do you measure and reduce an array's memory footprint?
questions.answer: `arr.nbytes` gives total bytes and `arr.itemsize` bytes per element. To reduce it: downcast to the smallest sufficient dtype (`float32` over `float64`, `int8` for small categorical codes) — often halving or quartering memory; avoid `object` dtype; use views instead of copies; operate in place with `arr += 1` or `np.add(a, b, out=a)`; and memory-map when the data lives on disk.

questions.question: Difference between C-order and F-order memory layout?
questions.answer: C-order (row-major, the NumPy default) stores each row contiguously, so iterating along the last axis is cache-friendly. F-order (column-major, as in Fortran/MATLAB/R) stores each column contiguously. The values are identical — only the traversal cost differs, which matters for large arrays and for handing data to Fortran-based libraries. Check with `arr.flags`; set with `np.array(x, order='F')`.

questions.question: What is the difference between np.copy(), .view() and plain assignment?
questions.answer: `b = a` binds another name to the *same* object — no new array at all. `b = a.view()` creates a new array object that shares the same data buffer, so writing to `b` changes `a` (basic slicing also returns views). `b = a.copy()` allocates a completely independent buffer. Check with `b.base is a` (a view) or `b.flags.owndata`.

questions.question: Difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy in NumPy?
questions.answer: A shallow copy (a view) duplicates the array metadata — shape, strides, dtype — but points at the original data buffer, so mutations propagate both ways. A deep copy (`arr.copy()` or `copy.deepcopy`) duplicates the data too, giving full independence at the cost of memory. The classic interview trap: `b = a[0:2]; b[0] = 99` also changes `a`, because slicing yields a view, not a copy — unlike Python list slicing.

questions.question: What are structured (record) arrays?
questions.answer: Arrays whose dtype defines several named fields of different types per element, like a database row: `np.array([('Ana', 25, 5.6)], dtype=[('name','U10'),('age','i4'),('ht','f8')])`. Access fields by name — `arr['age']`. Useful for heterogeneous fixed-schema data, though pandas is usually the better tool today.

questions.question: What is a masked array?
questions.answer: `np.ma.masked_array(data, mask)` pairs data with a boolean mask marking invalid entries. Aggregations then skip masked elements automatically — `np.ma.masked_invalid(a).mean()` ignores NaNs without you filtering first. It keeps the original shape intact, unlike boolean filtering which drops elements.

questions.question: What does arr.flags tell you, and what is np.ascontiguousarray()?
questions.answer: `arr.flags` reports memory properties: `C_CONTIGUOUS`, `F_CONTIGUOUS`, `OWNDATA` (does it own its buffer or is it a view), and `WRITEABLE`. Slicing with a step or transposing produces a non-contiguous array, which can slow down downstream operations or be rejected by C extensions — `np.ascontiguousarray(arr)` copies it into a fresh C-contiguous buffer.

questions.question: What is the difference between indexing and slicing? Does slicing copy the data?
questions.answer: Indexing retrieves individual elements — `arr[2]`, or `arr[1, 3]` in 2D. Slicing retrieves a range — `arr[1:4]`, `arr[:, 1:3]` — using `start:stop:step`. Crucially, basic slicing returns a **view**, not a copy, so modifying the slice modifies the original array. This differs from Python lists, where slicing copies. Call `.copy()` when you need independence.

questions.question: How is arr[:, 0] different from arr[:, [0]]?
questions.answer: `arr[:, 0]` uses an integer index, which drops that axis — the result is 1D with shape `(n,)`, and it is a view. `arr[:, [0]]` uses a list, which is fancy indexing that preserves the axis — the result is 2D with shape `(n, 1)`, and it is a copy. The shape difference matters enormously when the result feeds into broadcasting or matrix multiplication.

questions.question: What is the difference between basic indexing and advanced (fancy) indexing?
questions.answer: Basic indexing uses integers and slices and always returns a **view**. Advanced (fancy) indexing uses integer arrays/lists or boolean arrays and always returns a **copy**. Example: `arr[[0, 2, 4]]` selects those three rows into a new array; `arr[[0,1],[2,3]]` picks the elements at (0,2) and (1,3). The view-vs-copy distinction is the single most common NumPy interview trap.

questions.question: What is boolean indexing (masking)?
questions.answer: Using a boolean array of the same shape to select elements where the mask is True: `arr[arr > 5]` returns a flat array of the qualifying values. Combine conditions with `&`, `|` and `~` — **not** `and`/`or`/`not` — and always parenthesize: `arr[(arr > 5) & (arr < 10)]`. It also works for assignment: `arr[arr < 0] = 0` clips negatives in place.

questions.question: What is np.where() and how is it used?
questions.answer: It has two forms. With one argument, `np.where(cond)` returns a tuple of index arrays where the condition is True. With three, `np.where(cond, x, y)` is a vectorized if-else, picking from `x` where True and `y` where False — for example `np.where(scores >= 40, 'pass', 'fail')`. The three-argument form is the standard way to conditionally label data without a loop.

questions.question: Difference between np.where() and boolean indexing?
questions.answer: Boolean indexing `arr[arr > 5]` extracts the matching values, so the result is shorter than the input. `np.where(arr > 5)` returns their positions instead, and `np.where(arr > 5, a, b)` returns an array of the *same shape* with replacements. Use boolean indexing to filter, `np.where` to locate or to transform while preserving shape.

questions.question: What is np.select() and when is it better than np.where()?
questions.answer: `np.select([cond1, cond2, cond3], [val1, val2, val3], default=0)` evaluates several conditions in order and picks the value for the first match. It replaces deeply nested `np.where(c1, a, np.where(c2, b, ...))` chains, which become unreadable past two levels — the natural choice for multi-band bucketing like grade boundaries.

questions.question: What does np.nonzero() return?
questions.answer: A tuple of index arrays — one per dimension — giving the positions of all non-zero (or True) elements. For a 2D array it returns `(row_indices, col_indices)`, so you can do `arr[np.nonzero(arr)]`. `np.where(condition)` with a single argument is literally implemented as `np.nonzero(condition)`.

questions.question: How do you find the row and column positions of all elements greater than a value in a 2D array?
questions.answer: `np.argwhere(arr > 10)` returns an (N, 2) array where each row is an `[row, col]` coordinate pair — convenient for iterating over hits. `np.nonzero(arr > 10)` returns the same information transposed, as a tuple of two arrays, which is the form you need for direct fancy indexing.

questions.question: What do np.take() and np.put() do?
questions.answer: `np.take(arr, [0, 3, 5])` gathers elements at the given indices into a new array — equivalent to `arr[[0,3,5]]` but it works on a flattened view by default and accepts an `axis` and out-of-bounds `mode`. `np.put(arr, [0, 3], [99, 88])` writes values at the given flat positions **in place**. Both are handy when indices are computed programmatically.

questions.question: What do np.extract() and np.compress() do?
questions.answer: `np.extract(arr % 3 == 0, arr)` returns the elements satisfying a condition — the functional equivalent of `arr[arr % 3 == 0]`. `np.compress(condition, arr, axis=0)` selects whole slices along an axis where the condition holds, e.g. keeping only certain rows. Both are older API; boolean indexing is the idiomatic modern choice.

questions.question: What is np.searchsorted() used for?
questions.answer: It finds where a value should be inserted into a **sorted** array to keep it sorted — a binary search, so O(log n) instead of a linear scan. `np.searchsorted([1,3,5,7], 4)` returns `2`. It vectorizes over a list of values, and `side='left'/'right'` controls tie handling, which makes it the standard tool for bucketing continuous values into bins.

questions.question: How do you reverse a NumPy array? What is the difference between fliplr and flipud?
questions.answer: `arr[::-1]` reverses a 1D array (returning a view, not a copy). For multi-dimensional arrays, `np.flip(arr, axis=0)` reverses along a chosen axis. `np.flipud(arr)` flips up/down — reversing the row order, equivalent to `arr[::-1, :]`. `np.fliplr(arr)` flips left/right — reversing the column order, equivalent to `arr[:, ::-1]`. `fliplr` requires at least 2D.

questions.question: How do you reshape an array? What does -1 mean in reshape?
questions.answer: `arr.reshape(3, 4)` or `np.reshape(arr, (3, 4))` — the total element count must stay the same, so a 12-element array can become (3,4), (2,6) or (2,2,3). Passing `-1` for one dimension tells NumPy to infer it: `arr.reshape(-1, 3)` means 3 columns and however many rows are needed, and `arr.reshape(-1)` flattens. Reshaping returns a view when possible, so it is essentially free.

questions.question: Difference between np.reshape() and np.resize()?
questions.answer: `reshape` requires the element count to match exactly and errors otherwise, returning a view where possible. `np.resize(arr, new_shape)` will change the total size — repeating the data cyclically if the new shape is larger, truncating if smaller — and always returns a copy. The in-place method `arr.resize()` behaves differently again, padding with zeros.

questions.question: Difference between flatten() and ravel()?
questions.answer: Both collapse an array to 1D. `flatten()` always returns a **copy**, so it is safe but allocates memory. `ravel()` returns a **view** whenever the data is contiguous, so it is faster and memory-free — but writing to the result then modifies the original. Use `ravel()` for read-only flattening in performance-sensitive code, `flatten()` when you need independence.

questions.question: What are np.newaxis, np.expand_dims() and np.squeeze()?
questions.answer: `np.newaxis` (an alias for `None`) inserts a length-1 axis via indexing: `arr[:, np.newaxis]` turns shape `(3,)` into `(3, 1)`. `np.expand_dims(arr, axis=1)` does the same as a function call. `np.squeeze(arr)` removes all length-1 axes, turning `(1, 3, 1)` into `(3,)`. Adding an axis is the standard trick for making broadcasting line up — for instance turning a row vector into a column vector.

questions.question: What does the axis parameter mean? What is the difference between axis=0 and axis=1?
questions.answer: The axis is the dimension that gets **collapsed** by the operation. For a 2D array, `axis=0` runs down the rows and produces one result per column (a column-wise mean); `axis=1` runs across the columns and produces one result per row (a row-wise mean). Omitting `axis` aggregates over the entire flattened array. Remember it as: the axis you name is the one that disappears from the output shape.

questions.question: How do you transpose an array or interchange two axes?
questions.answer: `arr.T` or `np.transpose(arr)` reverses the axis order — for 2D this is the standard matrix transpose. For higher dimensions you can specify the permutation: `np.transpose(arr, (1, 0, 2))`. To swap exactly two axes, `np.swapaxes(arr, 0, 1)` is clearer, and `np.moveaxis(arr, 0, -1)` relocates one axis. All return views, so they are free.

questions.question: Difference between np.vstack(), np.hstack() and np.concatenate()?
questions.answer: `np.vstack((a, b))` stacks vertically, adding rows — equivalent to `np.concatenate((a, b), axis=0)`. `np.hstack((a, b))` stacks horizontally, adding columns — equivalent to `axis=1` for 2D arrays. `np.concatenate` is the general form requiring an explicit axis. All need the non-joining dimensions to match, and none of them modify the inputs — they allocate a new array.

questions.question: Difference between np.stack() and np.concatenate()?
questions.answer: `np.concatenate` joins arrays along an **existing** axis, so the result has the same number of dimensions. `np.stack` joins them along a **new** axis, adding a dimension: stacking three arrays of shape `(4,)` with `np.stack` gives `(3, 4)`, while `np.concatenate` gives `(12,)`. Use `stack` when you are building a batch out of individual samples.

questions.question: How do you split an array? What is the difference between split() and array_split()?
questions.answer: `np.split(arr, 3)` divides into three equal parts and raises a `ValueError` if the array does not divide evenly. `np.array_split(arr, 3)` handles uneven division gracefully, making the earlier sections one element larger. Convenience wrappers: `np.vsplit` splits along rows (axis 0), `np.hsplit` along columns (axis 1). You can also pass a list of indices to cut at specific positions.

questions.question: Difference between np.tile() and np.repeat()?
questions.answer: `np.repeat([1,2,3], 2)` duplicates each element in place → `[1,1,2,2,3,3]`. `np.tile([1,2,3], 2)` repeats the whole array as a block → `[1,2,3,1,2,3]`. `tile` also accepts a shape tuple to replicate in 2D. The classic exam variant — repeat each element five times — is `np.repeat(arr, 5)`.

questions.question: What is np.pad() used for? How do you add a border of zeros around an array?
questions.answer: `np.pad(arr, pad_width=1, mode='constant', constant_values=0)` wraps the array in a one-element border of zeros — a 3×3 array becomes 5×5. Other modes include `edge` (repeat boundary values), `reflect` and `wrap`. It is standard preprocessing before convolution, so the output keeps the input's spatial dimensions.

questions.question: What is np.meshgrid() used for?
questions.answer: It turns two 1D coordinate vectors into two 2D coordinate matrices covering the full grid: `X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)`. Every `(X[i,j], Y[i,j])` pair is one point on the plane, so you can evaluate a function over the whole surface in one vectorized expression — `Z = np.sin(X) + np.cos(Y)` — which is what contour plots, heatmaps and 3D surfaces need.

questions.question: What is broadcasting in NumPy?
questions.answer: The mechanism that lets NumPy apply element-wise operations to arrays of different shapes by virtually stretching the smaller one to match the larger — without physically copying data. `np.array([1,2,3]) + 10` adds 10 to each element; a `(3,4)` array plus a `(4,)` array adds that row to every row. It saves both memory and the explicit loop.

questions.question: What are the rules of broadcasting?
questions.answer: Compare shapes from the **trailing** (rightmost) dimension backwards. 1) If the arrays have different `ndim`, the smaller shape is left-padded with 1s. 2) Two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is 1 — in which case that array is stretched along it. 3) If any dimension pair is neither equal nor 1, broadcasting fails with a ValueError. Example: `(3,1)` with `(1,4)` broadcasts to `(3,4)`.

questions.question: Give an example of broadcasting a 2D array with a scalar and with a vector.
questions.answer: With a scalar: `arr * 2` — the scalar is treated as shape `()` and stretched across everything. With a row vector: a `(3,4)` array plus a `(4,)` array adds those four values to every row. With a column vector: `arr + col` where `col` has shape `(3,1)` adds one value per row. Mean-centering columns is the canonical use: `arr - arr.mean(axis=0)`.

questions.question: When does broadcasting fail, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: It fails when a dimension pair is neither equal nor 1 — a `(3,4)` array with a `(3,)` array raises `operands could not be broadcast together`, because the trailing dimensions 4 and 3 do not match. The fix is to add an explicit axis so the shapes align: `arr - col[:, np.newaxis]` turns `(3,)` into `(3,1)`, which then broadcasts across the four columns. Debug by printing `.shape` on both operands.

questions.question: What is vectorization in NumPy?
questions.answer: Expressing an operation over an entire array at once — `c = a * b` — instead of writing a Python `for` loop over the elements. The loop still happens, but inside compiled C with no interpreter overhead, no per-element type checks, and often SIMD instructions. It is both dramatically faster (typically 10-100×) and shorter to read. The rule of thumb: if you are writing a Python loop over a NumPy array, there is almost certainly a vectorized alternative.

questions.question: How is vectorization related to broadcasting?
questions.answer: They are complementary. Vectorization is *what* happens — an operation applied to whole arrays in compiled code. Broadcasting is *how* NumPy makes mismatched shapes compatible so the vectorized operation can run at all. Without broadcasting you would have to materialize a full-size copy of the smaller operand first, which wastes memory; broadcasting achieves the same result by manipulating strides.

questions.question: What are ufuncs (universal functions)?
questions.answer: Functions that operate element-wise on ndarrays, implemented in compiled C, with automatic broadcasting, type casting and an optional `out` parameter for in-place results. Unary ufuncs take one array (`np.sqrt`, `np.exp`, `np.abs`, `np.sin`); binary ufuncs take two (`np.add`, `np.multiply`, `np.maximum`). The arithmetic operators are just syntactic sugar over them — `a + b` calls `np.add`. Ufuncs also expose `.reduce()`, `.accumulate()` and `.outer()`.

questions.question: What is np.vectorize() and why is it not actually fast?
questions.answer: `np.vectorize(f)` wraps a scalar Python function so it accepts arrays and broadcasts. But the documentation is explicit that it is provided for convenience, not performance — internally it still calls your Python function once per element, so it is essentially a loop with nicer syntax. For real speed you must express the logic with existing ufuncs, `np.where`, or reach for Numba/Cython.

questions.question: How do you apply a custom function to each row or column of a 2D array?
questions.answer: `np.apply_along_axis(func, axis=1, arr=data)` runs the function on each 1D row slice (`axis=0` for columns). It is readable but still loops in Python. Whenever the function can be written with array operations, prefer the vectorized form with an axis argument — `data.mean(axis=1)` is far faster than applying a mean function row by row.

questions.question: How do you perform element-wise operations on arrays?
questions.answer: Use the ordinary operators directly on arrays of compatible shapes: `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` (element-wise product, **not** matrix multiplication), `a / b`, `a ** 2`, `a > b`. Equivalent ufunc forms are `np.add(a, b)`, `np.multiply(a, b)` and so on, which additionally accept `out=` for in-place results. The trap to remember: `*` is element-wise; use `@` or `np.dot` for matrix multiplication.

questions.question: How do you compute a moving average or rolling statistic in NumPy?
questions.answer: The simple approach is convolution: `np.convolve(arr, np.ones(w)/w, mode='valid')` gives a w-point moving average. A faster, allocation-free approach uses a cumulative sum: `c = np.cumsum(arr); (c[w:] - c[:-w]) / w`. The modern idiomatic way is `np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(arr, w).mean(axis=1)`, which creates a strided view of every window with no copying.

questions.question: How do you compute mean, median, standard deviation and variance?
questions.answer: `np.mean(arr)`, `np.median(arr)`, `np.std(arr)`, `np.var(arr)` — all accept an `axis` argument for row- or column-wise results. Important detail: NumPy defaults to the **population** standard deviation (`ddof=0`); pass `ddof=1` for the sample standard deviation, which is what pandas uses by default. That discrepancy is a favourite follow-up question.

questions.question: Difference between np.mean() and np.average()?
questions.answer: `np.mean()` computes the plain arithmetic mean. `np.average()` can do the same but additionally accepts a `weights` argument for a weighted mean: `np.average(scores, weights=credits)` computes a GPA. Use `mean` unless you need weighting; `average` also has a `returned=True` option that gives back the sum of weights.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum/minimum value and its index?
questions.answer: `np.max(arr)` and `np.min(arr)` return the values; `np.argmax(arr)` and `np.argmin(arr)` return the **flat index** of the first occurrence. For a 2D array pass `axis` for per-row/per-column results, and use `np.unravel_index(np.argmax(arr), arr.shape)` to convert the flat index back into `(row, col)` coordinates. Use `np.nanmax`/`np.nanargmax` when NaNs may be present.

questions.question: Difference between np.cumsum() and np.cumprod()?
questions.answer: `np.cumsum([1,2,3,4])` gives the running total `[1,3,6,10]`; `np.cumprod([1,2,3,4])` gives the running product `[1,2,6,24]`. Both preserve the input length, unlike `sum`/`prod` which collapse to a scalar. Cumulative sums are the trick behind fast sliding-window aggregates and empirical CDFs.

questions.question: What is np.clip() used for?
questions.answer: `np.clip(arr, 0, 255)` caps every value into the `[min, max]` range — anything below becomes 0, anything above becomes 255, and the array keeps its shape. It differs from filtering, which removes elements. Common uses: bounding pixel values, capping outliers without dropping rows, and preventing `log(0)` with `np.clip(p, 1e-9, 1)`.

questions.question: How do you handle NaN and infinite values in a NumPy array?
questions.answer: Detect with `np.isnan(arr)`, `np.isinf(arr)` or `np.isfinite(arr)`. Remove with `arr[~np.isnan(arr)]`, or replace with `arr[np.isnan(arr)] = 0` / `np.nan_to_num(arr, nan=0.0, posinf=1e10)`. To aggregate while ignoring them, use the nan-aware variants: `np.nanmean`, `np.nansum`, `np.nanstd`, `np.nanmax`. Remember `np.nan == np.nan` is False — always test with `np.isnan`.

questions.question: Why does dividing by zero in NumPy warn instead of raising an error?
questions.answer: NumPy follows IEEE 754 floating-point semantics: `1/0` yields `inf`, `-1/0` yields `-inf`, and `0/0` yields `nan`, with a RuntimeWarning. Halting on one bad element would be wrong for array-wide computation, so the invalid result is propagated and you clean it up afterwards. Control the behaviour with `np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore')` as a context manager, or `np.seterr()` globally.

questions.question: How do you count how many times a value appears in an array?
questions.answer: For one value: `np.count_nonzero(arr == 5)` or `(arr == 5).sum()`. For all values at once: `np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)` returns the distinct values with their frequencies — works for any dtype. `np.bincount(arr)` is faster but only accepts non-negative integers and returns counts indexed by value.

questions.question: How do you find the unique elements of an array?
questions.answer: `np.unique(arr)` returns the sorted distinct values. Its options do a lot of work: `return_counts=True` gives frequencies, `return_index=True` gives the first position of each unique value in the original array, and `return_inverse=True` gives the indices that reconstruct the original — which is exactly how you label-encode a categorical column.

questions.question: How do you normalize or min-max scale data with NumPy?
questions.answer: Min-max scaling to [0,1]: `(arr - arr.min()) / (arr.max() - arr.min())`. Standardization (z-score): `(arr - arr.mean()) / arr.std()`. For a 2D feature matrix, scale per column with `axis=0` and keep the shape aligned via broadcasting: `(X - X.min(axis=0)) / (X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0))`. Guard against a zero range, and in ML always fit the statistics on the training set only.

questions.question: How do you compute Mean Squared Error with NumPy?
questions.answer: `mse = np.mean((y_true - y_pred) ** 2)` — one vectorized line, no loop. RMSE is `np.sqrt(mse)`, MAE is `np.mean(np.abs(y_true - y_pred))`. This question checks that you reach for broadcasting and aggregation rather than iterating over predictions.

questions.question: How do you identify outliers in a NumPy array?
questions.answer: Standard-deviation method: flag points more than k (typically 3) standard deviations from the mean — `mask = np.abs(arr - arr.mean()) > 3 * arr.std()`. IQR method, which is robust to the outliers themselves: `q1, q3 = np.percentile(arr, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1`, then flag anything outside `[q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr]`. Prefer IQR for skewed data, since extreme values inflate the mean and std.

questions.question: How do you compare two arrays? Why use np.allclose() instead of ==?
questions.answer: `arr1 == arr2` returns an element-wise boolean array, not a single verdict — reduce it with `.all()`. `np.array_equal(a, b)` checks shape and every element at once. For floats, exact equality is unreliable because binary representation makes `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`; use `np.allclose(a, b)` (or `np.isclose` element-wise), which compares within a relative and absolute tolerance.

questions.question: How do you compute the dot product of two arrays?
questions.answer: `np.dot(a, b)` or the `@` operator. For two 1D arrays it is the scalar inner product — `np.dot([1,2,3],[4,5,6])` gives 32. For 2D arrays it performs matrix multiplication. `np.inner` and `np.vdot` are related variants, and `np.cross(a, b)` gives the vector cross product.

questions.question: Difference between *, np.dot() and np.matmul() / @ ?
questions.answer: `a * b` is element-wise multiplication (the Hadamard product) and requires broadcast-compatible shapes. `np.dot` and `np.matmul`/`@` perform matrix multiplication and agree for 1D and 2D inputs. They diverge for higher dimensions: `matmul` broadcasts over the leading dimensions and treats the last two axes as the matrices (stacks of matrices), whereas `dot` computes a sum-product over the last axis of `a` and the second-to-last of `b`. `@` is the recommended modern form. Also, `np.dot` accepts scalars; `matmul` does not.

questions.question: How do you multiply two matrices in NumPy?
questions.answer: `A @ B`, `np.matmul(A, B)` or `np.dot(A, B)`. The inner dimensions must agree — an `(m, n)` matrix times an `(n, p)` matrix gives `(m, p)`. Remember `A * B` is **not** matrix multiplication; it multiplies element by element and will silently give you the wrong answer whenever the shapes happen to be broadcast-compatible.

questions.question: How do you invert a matrix?
questions.answer: `np.linalg.inv(A)` — the matrix must be square and non-singular (non-zero determinant), otherwise it raises `LinAlgError: Singular matrix`. Verify with `A @ np.linalg.inv(A)` being close to the identity (use `np.allclose`, not `==`). For solving equations, never invert explicitly — `np.linalg.solve` is faster and numerically more stable. `np.linalg.pinv` gives the pseudo-inverse for singular or non-square matrices.

questions.question: How do you compute the determinant of a matrix?
questions.answer: `np.linalg.det(A)` for a square matrix. A determinant of 0 means the matrix is singular and has no inverse. Because it is computed in floating point, a mathematically-zero determinant often comes back as something like `1e-17` — check with a tolerance rather than `== 0`, or better, use `np.linalg.matrix_rank` or `np.linalg.cond` to judge invertibility.

questions.question: How do you find eigenvalues and eigenvectors?
questions.answer: `vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)` returns both; `np.linalg.eigvals(A)` returns only the eigenvalues. The eigenvectors come back as **columns** of `vecs`, so the i-th eigenvector is `vecs[:, i]` — a very common indexing mistake. For symmetric or Hermitian matrices use `np.linalg.eigh`, which is faster and returns real, sorted eigenvalues. Eigen-decomposition underpins PCA.

questions.question: How do you solve a system of linear equations?
questions.answer: `x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)` solves `Ax = b` directly using LU decomposition. Prefer it over `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`, which is both slower and numerically less stable. For over-determined or inconsistent systems (more equations than unknowns), use `np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)` for the least-squares solution.

questions.question: What do np.trace() and np.diag() do?
questions.answer: `np.trace(A)` sums the main diagonal elements. `np.diag()` is overloaded by input rank: given a 2D matrix it **extracts** the diagonal as a 1D array; given a 1D array it **builds** a square matrix with those values on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. `np.diagonal(A)` and `A.diagonal(offset=k)` extract shifted diagonals.

questions.question: What matrix decompositions does NumPy provide?
questions.answer: `np.linalg.qr(A)` gives the QR decomposition (orthogonal Q, upper-triangular R) used in least-squares solving. `np.linalg.svd(A)` gives the singular value decomposition U·Σ·Vᵀ, the backbone of PCA, dimensionality reduction, low-rank approximation and pseudo-inverses. `np.linalg.cholesky(A)` decomposes a positive-definite matrix and is the fastest option when it applies.

questions.question: How do you generate random numbers in NumPy?
questions.answer: Modern API: `rng = np.random.default_rng(42)`, then `rng.random((3,3))` for uniform [0,1), `rng.integers(1, 100, size=10)` for integers, `rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=100)` for a Gaussian, `rng.choice(arr, size=5, replace=False)` for sampling. The legacy equivalents are `np.random.rand`, `np.random.randint`, `np.random.randn` and `np.random.choice`.

questions.question: Why set a random seed? Difference between np.random.seed() and np.random.default_rng()?
questions.answer: Seeding makes a pseudo-random sequence reproducible, which is essential for debugging, sharing results and fair model comparison. `np.random.seed(42)` sets one **global** state, so any library call can consume from it and change your results unpredictably. `np.random.default_rng(42)` returns an independent Generator object with its own state — no global side effects, better statistical quality, and safe for parallel work. Prefer the Generator API in new code.

questions.question: How do you shuffle an array or draw a random sample?
questions.answer: `rng.shuffle(arr)` shuffles **in place** along the first axis (so it reorders rows of a 2D array, not individual elements). `rng.permutation(arr)` returns a shuffled copy and leaves the original alone. For sampling, `rng.choice(arr, size=k, replace=False)` draws without repetition. To shuffle features and labels together, permute an index array once and apply it to both: `p = rng.permutation(len(X)); X[p], y[p]`.

questions.question: How do you sort an array in ascending and descending order?
questions.answer: `np.sort(arr)` returns a sorted copy in ascending order; `arr.sort()` sorts in place. There is no `reverse` parameter — for descending order use `np.sort(arr)[::-1]` or `-np.sort(-arr)`. For 2D arrays pass `axis` (`axis=1` sorts each row independently, `axis=None` flattens first), and `kind='stable'` when ties must preserve their original order.

questions.question: What is np.argsort() and how do you sort a 2D array by one column?
questions.answer: `np.argsort(arr)` returns the **indices** that would sort the array, rather than the sorted values. That indirection is what lets you reorder a whole table by one column: `data[np.argsort(data[:, 2])]` sorts every row by the third column, keeping rows intact. For multi-key sorting use `np.lexsort((secondary, primary))` — note the last key is the primary one.

questions.question: How do you find the N largest or smallest elements efficiently?
questions.answer: `np.partition(arr, -N)` performs a partial sort in O(n) rather than O(n log n), guaranteeing the N largest end up in the last N slots (unordered among themselves) — `np.partition(arr, -3)[-3:]`. `np.argpartition` gives the corresponding indices, which is how you get the top-k predictions from a score vector without sorting the whole thing.

questions.question: How do you perform set operations on NumPy arrays?
questions.answer: `np.union1d(a, b)` for the union, `np.intersect1d(a, b)` for common elements, `np.setdiff1d(a, b)` for elements in `a` but not `b`, and `np.setxor1d(a, b)` for the symmetric difference. All return sorted unique values. `np.isin(a, b)` is the element-wise membership test, returning a boolean mask the same shape as `a` — the vectorized equivalent of Python's `in`.

questions.question: How do you find local peaks (maxima) in a 1D array?
questions.answer: A peak is any element greater than both neighbours, so compare shifted slices: `peaks = np.where((arr[1:-1] > arr[:-2]) & (arr[1:-1] > arr[2:]))[0] + 1` — the `+1` corrects for the offset introduced by trimming the first element. An equivalent approach uses the sign of the first difference: `np.diff(np.sign(np.diff(arr)))` is negative exactly at a peak.

questions.question: How do you extract a subarray, add a zero border, and repeat elements — the classic coding tasks?
questions.answer: Subarray: `arr[1:4, 2:5]` slices rows 1-3 and columns 2-4 (a view). Zero border: `np.pad(arr, 1, mode='constant', constant_values=0)`. Repeat each element five times: `np.repeat(arr, 5)`. Interchange two axes: `np.swapaxes(arr, 0, 1)`. Integer array in a range: `np.arange(10, 61)`. These recur verbatim as the written-round questions on most banks.

questions.question: How would you implement K-Means using only NumPy?
questions.answer: Initialize k centroids by sampling rows: `C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]`. Then loop: compute all point-to-centroid distances with broadcasting — `d = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :], axis=2)` giving an (n, k) matrix; assign each point with `labels = d.argmin(axis=1)`; recompute each centroid as `X[labels == j].mean(axis=0)`; stop when the centroids stop moving (`np.allclose`). The interviewer is checking that you use broadcasting to avoid a double loop.

Every MOST_FREQ in that range is must-know — broadcasting and view-vs-copy are near-guaranteed.
study_plan.mid_level_2_to_5_yrs: Add Q23–Q32 (dtypes, memory layout, views, masked arrays), Q38–Q44 (the full querying API), Q53–Q57 (stack vs concatenate, split, tile vs repeat, pad, meshgrid), Q65–Q68 (np.vectorize's limits, apply_along_axis, moving averages), Q74–Q81 (NaN handling, normalization, outliers, allclose) and Q91–Q97. Be ready to explain *why* a vectorized version is faster, not just that it is.
study_plan.senior_5_plus_yrs: All 100 + follow-ups on memory-mapping and large-array strategy (Q22, Q26), C vs F contiguity and stride tricks (Q27, Q32, Q68), matmul vs dot in >2 dimensions (Q83), numerical stability in linear algebra (Q85, Q86, Q88), decompositions and PCA (Q87, Q90), and implementing an algorithm like K-Means with pure broadcasting (Q100).
